title: My daughter bought a used minivan for $6,000. The next morning, four strangers showed up offering her $200,000 to give it back (PART 2)

blocks.text: I hadn't had a first child. Not that I knew of. I'd had one daughter, Megan, born after a long, frightening labor at a private birthing center outside Denver. I'd been heavily sedated at the end. My husband, who passed away nine years ago, had always said the delivery was "complicated" and that I was lucky to come home with a healthy baby.

The detective turned the laptop toward me and played the video forward. A second baby was born four minutes after the first. A nurse wrapped her in a pink blanket and carried her out a side door while I lay unconscious.

The birthing center, closed since 2009, had been run by a respected obstetrician named Dr. Leland Voss. Investigators later found that, for more than a decade, he had quietly taken one baby from some multiple births and sold them through a private adoption lawyer to wealthy families who wanted to skip waiting lists.
Parents were told only one baby had survived, or never told about the second baby at all. He recorded every birth, apparently as insurance against his own staff.

Voss died in 2021. His son inherited the hard drives and kept them in a locked case, terrified of what was on them. The four men in suits were lawyers and investigators working for the son. The frozen bank account and the call to Megan's job were their attempt to pressure her into giving the van back before anyone looked under the seat.
Here is the part I still can't tell without crying. The private seller who sold Megan the van for six thousand dollars was named Rachel.
Rachel had grown up in California with adoptive parents who loved her. Last year, an ancestry DNA test matched her to a woman in Colorado: Megan.

Rachel dug into her adoption, found Voss's name, and eventually tracked down his son. She'd been cleaning his house as a temp worker for three weeks when she found the case of hard drives, took it, and hid it in a van she bought for cash, with the VIN plate swapped so it couldn't easily be traced.

She didn't know how to tell her twin sister, a stranger, that she existed. So she put the ad for the van where Megan would see it, priced it too low to refuse, and planned to tell her everything a week later. She just wanted the evidence somewhere safe, in the hands of the person it belonged to.
When the police called the number on the bill of sale, Rachel answered on the first ring. She'd been waiting for that call.
Megan and Rachel met at our kitchen table that night.

They have the same laugh. The same habit of tucking their hair behind their left ear. They sat across from each other in silence for a while, and then Megan said, "Do you want to see your room? I mean, we'd have to share." And they both started laughing and couldn't stop.

Voss's son was charged with obstruction and evidence tampering, and the adoption lawyer, now in his eighties, was charged with fraud. Investigators have identified eleven other families from the videos. Each of them has been contacted, carefully, one at a time.
Megan kept the van. She drives her sister to work in it every Tuesday.
